To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) pigeons can postpone TO from an ongoing variable-interval schedule of food delivery by making responses on a second key and that (b) this postponement is enhanced by the addition of stimuli correlated with the greatest distance from TO
the added stimuli functioned as discriminative stimuli, delineating periods when behavior was most effective in postponing TO, and that TO was aversive.
the time-correlated discriminative stimuli in our procedures serve to delineate periods during which responding is most effective in postponing TO.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role that discriminative stimuli play in the development and maintenance of avoidance behavior in the pigeon.
the discriminative control of the timing of TO in the absence of shock and with the effects of added stimuli that partition the TO period into discrete time segments.
the role of discriminative stimuli in the control of avoidance behavior.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results from the present studies are in accord with those obtained in the shock-avoidance paradigm.
the added stimuli are used by pigeons as discriminative stimuli in a procedure that is a variant of a shock-avoidance procedure.
the discriminative stimuli function to delineate periods in time during which the TO contingency is effective, and the postponement responses function to avoid TO.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
TO avoidance in pigeons, like shock avoidance in rats, involves both stimulus control and temporal control.
TO functions as a stimulus with properties similar to shock and that these properties can be altered by discriminative stimuli.
the added stimuli serve as discriminative stimuli that allow the animal to maximize the rate of reinforcement during the TO-avoidance schedule.
The main takeaway from our work is that
pigeons are capable of using the temporal structure of a TO period to discriminate periods of TO that are most effective in avoiding the aversive stimulus.
pigeons can learn to postpone TO by responding on a second key.

the TO-avoidance procedures are a viable alternative for studying the aversive properties of TO and the effects of added stimuli on the behavior of pigeons and other animals. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2019 APA, all rights reserved)
